CF-0.405.heading: CF-0.405: Forums Registry and Identifier Rules

CF-0.410.heading: CF-0.410: Scope, Authority, and Boundary Rules

CF-23.405.heading: CF-23.405: Forum Formation, Forum-Structure Mapping, and Chamber Structure
CF-23.405.gloss: Chapter Twenty-Three names the forum families; **CF-23.405** is where an adopting entity turns those names into working benches, chambers, and support structures. It sets the minimum each family must actually staff and run, keeps families from quietly collapsing into one another, and states what a chamber may and may not decide.

CF-23.405 §1.heading: CF-23.405 §1 Core Structural Rule
CF-23.405 §1.gloss: Every adopting entity must publish a real, working structure for each forum family — not a name on an organization chart. A filer must be able to tell which body handles what.

CF-23.405 §2.heading: CF-23.405 §2 Family-to-Forum-Structure Translation Map
CF-23.405 §2.gloss: A published map showing which actual body does the work of each constitutional forum family, and how it is organized — one standing body, several regional ones, or tiers.

CF-23.405 §3.heading: CF-23.405 §3 Family Distinction and Non-Collapse Rule
CF-23.405 §3.gloss: Families may share staff, buildings, and software and still must stay constitutionally distinct. Shared plumbing is not a reason to merge functions that are meant to check one another.

CF-23.405 §4.heading: CF-23.405 §4 Minimum Structural Availability by Family
CF-23.405 §4.gloss: Each family needs enough adjudicators and clerical support to actually function, so the same small group is not hearing everything.

CF-23.405 §5.heading: CF-23.405 §5 Chamber Creation, Identification, and Family Boundary
CF-23.405 §5.gloss: A family may create specialized chambers, but the instrument creating one must say which family it sits in and what it covers. A chamber never outranks its family boundary.

CF-23.405 §6.heading: CF-23.405 §6 Chamber Authority Composition and Service Mechanics
CF-23.405 §6.gloss: Who sits on a chamber, and how they are appointed and serve, must meet the shared floor for delegated binding bodies rather than being arranged case by case.

CF-23.405 §7.heading: CF-23.405 §7 Chamber Appeals, Review, and Routing Limits
CF-23.405 §7.gloss: Each chamber must state up front how its rulings can be reviewed. A chamber may not rewrite routing by habit or quietly take work that belongs to another family.

CF-23.405 §8.heading: CF-23.405 §8 Specialist and Technical Chamber Discipline
CF-23.405 §8.gloss: Creating a specialist chamber requires explaining why ordinary family-level handling will not do. Specialization must be justified, not assumed.

CF-23.410.heading: CF-23.410: Panel Formation, Disclosure, Recusal, and Lawful Bench Constitution
CF-23.410.gloss: **CF-23.410** decides who is allowed to sit on a case. It states what makes a panel lawful and independent, what must be disclosed before anyone touches the merits, when a member must step aside, and what happens when no independent panel can be formed at all.

CF-23.410 §1.heading: CF-23.410 §1 Lawful Panel Definitions
CF-23.410 §1.gloss: The vocabulary for the rest of the file: what counts as a panel member, and what makes a bench lawful.

CF-23.410 §10.heading: CF-23.410 §10 Certifier for Inability-to-Form Findings
CF-23.410 §10.gloss: Someone specific and independent must sign the finding that no lawful panel can be formed, and give reasons — otherwise the finding becomes an easy escape hatch.

CF-23.410 §11.heading: CF-23.410 §11 Backup-Forum Activation
CF-23.410 §11.gloss: Once inability-to-form is certified or the lead family is compromised, moving the matter to the backup family is mandatory, not discretionary.

CF-23.410 §12.heading: CF-23.410 §12 Interim Relief While Panel Independence Is Disputed
CF-23.410 §12.gloss: While the fight over who may hear the case continues, a provisional authority may still act — but only to stop irreversible harm, preserve evidence, or protect safety.

CF-23.410 §13.heading: CF-23.410 §13 Required Records for Panel Formation and Recusal
CF-23.410 §13.gloss: The paperwork that lets someone reconstruct later how this particular bench came to hear this particular case.

CF-23.410 §15.heading: CF-23.410 §15 Interim Hold on a Panel Member or Seat Holder

CF-23.410 §2.heading: CF-23.410 §2 Minimum Lawful-Panel Requirements
CF-23.410 §2.gloss: Each family must publish its own panel rules in advance — how many members, what counts as quorum, what expertise each seat needs, and who replaces whom. Deciding this after a case arrives invites manipulation.

CF-23.410 §3.heading: CF-23.410 §3 Publication and Pre-Assignment Transparency
CF-23.410 §3.gloss: How members are picked must be public before a case arrives, along with how to object to a given assignment.

CF-23.410 §4.heading: CF-23.410 §4 Mandatory Disclosures Before Merits Participation
CF-23.410 §4.gloss: Before touching the merits, a proposed member must disclose anything that could reasonably raise a question about impartiality — financial interest, close relationships, prior involvement.

CF-23.410 §5.heading: CF-23.410 §5 Recusal Triggers
CF-23.410 §5.gloss: The situations where stepping aside is required rather than optional, including having already acted in the matter in another role.

CF-23.410 §6.heading: CF-23.410 §6 Recusal Challenge Workflow
CF-23.410 §6.gloss: A usable route for a party to say "this member should not be hearing my case" — in plain language, with a decision that can itself be reviewed.

CF-23.410 §7.heading: CF-23.410 §7 Strategic or Abusive Recusal
CF-23.410 §7.gloss: Recusal cuts both ways. Stepping aside to dodge a politically awkward case, to create delay, or to steer a matter to a preferred substitute is itself misconduct.

CF-23.410 §8.heading: CF-23.410 §8 Replacement and Substitute Selection
CF-23.410 §8.gloss: Replacements follow a published order rather than being hand-picked for the case, and a substitute carrying the same conflict is no substitute.

CF-23.410 §9.heading: CF-23.410 §9 Inability to Form an Independent Panel
CF-23.410 §9.gloss: What it means when a family genuinely cannot assemble a clean bench — too many conflicts, cascading recusals, capture indicators, or deadlock over composition.

CF-23.415.heading: CF-23.415: Routing Operations, Transfer, Questions for Ruling, and Representative Treatment
CF-23.415.gloss: **CF-23.415** is day-to-day traffic control for cases — how a matter is classified on arrival, who triages it, when it may be transferred, and how anyone acting on another's behalf must be treated. Routing must be published and reviewable, so a case cannot be steered to a friendly venue in silence.

CF-23.415 §1.heading: CF-23.415 §1 Published Intake Classes
CF-23.415 §1.gloss: Every family must publish how it sorts incoming matters by urgency, with at least three levels, and add finer sorting when volume demands it.

CF-23.415 §2.heading: CF-23.415 §2 Intake Triage Body
CF-23.415 §2.gloss: Somebody must own the first touch — sorting arrivals into the published classes — and that role carries the same independence and challenge expectations as the rest of the process.

CF-23.415 §3.heading: CF-23.415 §3 Natural-Systems Representatives
CF-23.415 §3.gloss: An Environment forum case protecting a life-supporting system's own continuity may be opened by a published representative — an affected community, indigenous-continuity holder, or designated guardian — without treating the system as a sentient.

CF-23.420.heading: CF-23.420: Appeal, Secondary Review, and Exhaustion Pathways
CF-23.420.gloss: **CF-23.420** makes sure a first decision is not automatically the last word. It sets the minimum review routes every forum family must keep open, labels what each disposition actually decided, and stops "you have not exhausted your options" from being used to run out the clock.

CF-23.420 §1.heading: CF-23.420 §1 Disposition-Effect Categories and Record Labels
CF-23.420 §1.gloss: Labels stating how far a ruling reaches: only these parties, a whole class, later panels, or a technical standard. Recording the reach prevents a narrow decision from quietly becoming a general rule.

CF-23.420 §2.heading: CF-23.420 §2 Core Rules
CF-23.420 §2.gloss: The floor for review: a route that is understandable, usable without unreasonable obstacles, and fast enough to fix a serious error while the remedy still means something.

CF-23.420 §2.2.heading: CF-23.420 §2.2 Emergency, Exhaustion, and Timing Rules

CF-23.420 §2.4.heading: CF-23.420 §2.4 Sanctions, Restrictions, and Corrective Measures

CF-23.420 §2.5.heading: CF-23.420 §2.5 Appeal Outcomes, Remedies, and Reviewable Forum Case Records

CF-23.425.heading: CF-23.425: Integrity Safeguards, Anti-Capture Operations, and Anti-Self-Judging Support
CF-23.425.gloss: **CF-23.425** stops a body from judging its own conduct, and stops an interested party from quietly capturing the body that reviews it. It covers alignment rulings, when a matter must be routed away from a compromised venue, and what happens when a whole forum family is compromised rather than a single member.

CF-23.425 §1.heading: CF-23.425 §1 Alignment Rulings, Component Referral, and Supervisory Coordination
CF-23.425 §1.gloss: How an Integrity forum handles a tangled, multi-part problem: keep one lead record, send each component to the body that properly owns it, and coordinate without absorbing everyone else's jurisdiction.

CF-23.425 §1.2.heading: CF-23.425 §1.2 Component Referral and Priority Publication

CF-23.425 §1.4.heading: CF-23.425 §1.4 Merits Boundaries and Referred-Forum Authority

CF-23.425 §2.heading: CF-23.425 §2 Constitutional Alignment Certification and Review
CF-23.425 §2.gloss: How a system gets officially recognized as constitutionally aligned within a stated scope, and how that recognition is rechecked later. Recognition is contestable and does not expire into a permanent seal of approval.

CF-23.425 §2.6.heading: CF-23.425 §2.6 Component Referrals and Questions for Ruling

CF-23.425 §3.heading: CF-23.425 §3 Anti-Self-Judging Activation, Capture-Sensitive Routing, Contest-Integrity Interfaces, and Family-Level Capture
CF-23.425 §3.gloss: The machinery for moving a matter away from a body that cannot judge it impartially — including the severe case where an entire forum family, not just one member, has been compromised.

CF-23.425 §3.3.heading: CF-23.425 §3.3 Backup Family Map and Limits

CF-23.425 §3.5.heading: CF-23.425 §3.5 Internal Integrity Process and Forum Access

CF-23.430.heading: CF-23.430: Forum Forensic and Analytical Support
CF-23.430.gloss: **CF-23.430** gives a forum access to qualified technical help when the facts are too specialized, hidden, or tangled to weigh unaided. That help explains the evidence; it does not decide the case, prosecute it, or become a second forum.

CF-23.430 §1.heading: CF-23.430 §1 When Forensic or Analytical Support Is Required
CF-23.430 §1.gloss: The situations where a forum must be able to call for technical help: the evidence is fragmented, restricted, highly technical, or the uncertainty could change the outcome.

CF-23.430 §2.heading: CF-23.430 §2 What Support Personnel May Do
CF-23.430 §2.gloss: Titles vary — inspector, analyst, special master — but the scope must be written down, and the record must make clear to the parties what that person was asked to do.

CF-23.430 §3.heading: CF-23.430 §3 Independence, Conflicts, and Challenges
CF-23.430 §3.gloss: Technical helpers face the same conflict screening as decision-makers, and parties must have a real way to challenge who was appointed.

CF-23.430 §4.heading: CF-23.430 §4 Evidence Custody and Method Records
CF-23.430 §4.gloss: The trail a later reviewer needs: what was tested, how, by whom, what was uncertain, and where the gaps are.

CF-23.430 §5.heading: CF-23.430 §5 Reports, Explanations, and Emergency Preservation
CF-23.430 §5.gloss: Findings must be understandable to an ordinary affected sentient without dumbing down the technical substance. Acting without notice is allowed only when delay would destroy the evidence.

CF-23.430 §6.heading: CF-23.430 §6 Boundary with Contest-Integrity Monitoring
CF-23.430 §6.gloss: Two related jobs kept separate: **CF-23.430** builds the evidence record for one case; contest-integrity monitoring asks whether the system is working across many cases.

CF-23.435.heading: CF-23.435: Independent Investigative Service and Prosecution Interface
CF-23.435.gloss: **CF-23.435** requires investigators independent enough to follow the facts wherever they lead, and keeps investigating a matter separate from deciding to charge, sanction, or close it. No body may investigate itself.

CF-23.435 §2.heading: CF-23.435 §2 Why Independence Matters
CF-23.435 §2.gloss: The reasoning in one line: whoever may have caused the problem must not control the investigation into it.

CF-23.435 §3.heading: CF-23.435 §3 Where the Investigative Service Belongs
CF-23.435 §3.gloss: Investigators must sit in a protected line of their own, not under the same command as the enforcement or prosecution they may need to examine.

CF-23.435 §4.heading: CF-23.435 §4 What Investigators May Do
CF-23.435 §4.gloss: The authority to take complaints, gather and preserve evidence, interview, and prepare a reasoned packet for whoever decides what happens next.

CF-23.435 §5.heading: CF-23.435 §5 Required Separations
CF-23.435 §5.gloss: Several bodies may contribute to one matter, but each stays in its lane — investigating, charging, and deciding must not collapse into a single hand.

CF-23.435 §5.1.heading: CF-23.435 §5.1 Non-Forum Investigative, Security-Support, and Enforcement Roles

CF-23.435 §6.heading: CF-23.435 §6 No Self-Investigation
CF-23.435 §6.gloss: No body keeps sole control of an inquiry into its own misconduct. Where the allegations reach the usual investigators, the matter must go elsewhere.

CF-23.435 §7.heading: CF-23.435 §7 Rights, Secrecy, and Protected Activity
CF-23.435 §7.gloss: Investigations may sometimes need sealed steps and delayed notice, but secrecy stays bounded by necessity, proportionality, and oversight — it is not a blanket exemption.

CF-23.435 §8.heading: CF-23.435 §8 Records, Referrals, and Backup Routes
CF-23.435 §8.gloss: The record must state scope, steps, evidence, uncertainty, and reasons — including evidence that cuts against the investigators' own theory — so a closure decision can be checked.

CF-23.440.heading: CF-23.440: Technical Specialist Forums and Specialist Chambers
CF-23.440.gloss: **CF-23.440** lets a system use scientific, engineering, and medical expertise without letting that expertise harden into an unaccountable parallel judiciary. Specialist bodies sit inside the Chapter Twenty-Three families, publish the standards they apply, and stay reviewable.

CF-23.440 §10.heading: CF-23.440 §10 Departure and Variance
CF-23.440 §10.gloss: Published shared standards bind within their adopted scope. Departing from one requires a justified, recorded variance; treating a standard as merely aspirational is not an option.

CF-23.440 §11.heading: CF-23.440 §11 Cross-Jurisdiction Recognition
CF-23.440 §11.gloss: A standard already worked out elsewhere is presumptively recognized rather than relitigated from scratch, unless there is a stated reason it does not fit.

CF-23.440 §12.heading: CF-23.440 §12 Educational Materials and Textbook Disputes
CF-23.440 §12.gloss: In curriculum disputes the question is evidence integrity and honest presentation, not which conclusion the body prefers.

CF-23.440 §13.heading: CF-23.440 §13 Independence and Composition
CF-23.440 §13.gloss: Panels need genuine domain competence plus terms and pay that do not leave members dependent on the funders, journals, or vendors whose work they review.

CF-23.440 §14.heading: CF-23.440 §14 Research and Uncertainty-Reduction Authority
CF-23.440 §14.gloss: A specialist body may commission research, but only after publishing a finding that the existing uncertainty is actually blocking reliable decisions.

CF-23.440 §15.heading: CF-23.440 §15 Publication and Review Governance
CF-23.440 §15.gloss: Where the dispute involves suppressed publication, refused replication, or blocked correction, this file is read together with the institutional rules on scientific publication.

CF-23.440 §2.heading: CF-23.440 §2 Purpose
CF-23.440 §2.gloss: Why these bodies exist: to give expert-evidence questions a reviewable home, so expertise informs decisions without becoming an authority no one can question.

CF-23.440 §3.heading: CF-23.440 §3 Core Functions
CF-23.440 §3.gloss: Mainly setting and revising the standards other bodies use for expert evidence — reproducibility, uncertainty, replication status, and what counts as sufficient proof.

CF-23.440 §4.heading: CF-23.440 §4 Required Chamber Coverage
CF-23.440 §4.gloss: The specialist chambers an adopting instrument should provide at minimum, such as science, engineering, and medical.

CF-23.440 §5.heading: CF-23.440 §5 Optional Additional Chambers
CF-23.440 §5.gloss: Other domains that may warrant their own chamber where expert-evidence questions recur — ecology, education, statistics, and comparable fields.

CF-23.440 §6.heading: CF-23.440 §6 Routing and Limits
CF-23.440 §6.gloss: Specialist bodies take questions where the expert method is the real dispute. They do not become a general venue by absorbing cases that belong elsewhere.

CF-23.440 §7.heading: CF-23.440 §7 Standard-Setting Constraints
CF-23.440 §7.gloss: Published standards must separate what the evidence shows from what someone chose as policy, and must leave room for credible minority and emerging views rather than freezing one school in place.

CF-23.440 §8.heading: CF-23.440 §8 Shared Standards and Decentralized Enforcement
CF-23.440 §8.gloss: One body maintains a shared standard; many bodies apply it. Maintenance is centralized so the standard stays coherent, enforcement stays distributed so it stays accountable.

CF-23.440 §9.heading: CF-23.440 §9 Institutional-Forum Interface
CF-23.440 §9.gloss: When a technical standard is used against an institution, the case is normally heard by the Institutional family — the standard is technical, but the dispute is about institutional conduct.

CF-23.445.heading: CF-23.445: Forum Performance, Backlog Requirements, Publication Timeliness, and Accessibility
CF-23.445.gloss: **CF-23.445** treats delay and inaccessibility as constitutional failures rather than administrative inconvenience. A forum that formally exists but is too slow, too opaque, or too hard to use is not doing its job, so this file sets what must be measured, the thresholds that trigger alarm, and the fixes required once one is crossed.

CF-23.445 §1.heading: CF-23.445 §1 Core Rule
CF-23.445 §1.gloss: Performance is measured by what an affected party can actually do: find out where the matter stands, reach a forum without unreasonable delay, and challenge a decision while the remedy still matters.

CF-23.445 §10.heading: CF-23.445 §10 Lived Conditions during Restriction and Re-Entry Alignment (Cross-Layer)
CF-23.445 §10.gloss: Where a matter involves coercive or containment conditions, forum timing must be checked against the systems-layer floors for lived conditions. Good calendar numbers do not excuse bad conditions.

CF-23.445 §2.heading: CF-23.445 §2 Urgency-Scaled Service Requirements (Notice through Remediation Closure)
CF-23.445 §2.gloss: Timing requirements scale with urgency and cover the whole span — from first notice through to remediation actually being closed out, not merely ordered.

CF-23.445 §3.heading: CF-23.445 §3 Metric Registry and Reporting Taxonomy
CF-23.445 §3.gloss: The single list of what every forum family must measure and publish. Later sections apply these categories rather than inventing parallel ones.

CF-23.445 §3.1.heading: CF-23.445 §3.1 Stage Targets and Outer Bounds

CF-23.445 §4.heading: CF-23.445 §4 Performance Thresholds and Alerts
CF-23.445 §4.gloss: Each family sets the numbers at which a measure stops being a statistic and becomes an alarm — aging, backlog, accuracy, publication failure, and constitutional risk.

CF-23.445 §5.heading: CF-23.445 §5 Required Remediation Actions for Threshold Crossings
CF-23.445 §5.gloss: Crossing a threshold obliges an attributable record and a fix, so a breach cannot be absorbed silently into the next reporting period.

CF-23.445 §6.heading: CF-23.445 §6 Forum-Performance Review Cadence
CF-23.445 §6.gloss: Performance must be reviewed on a fixed schedule and compared against earlier periods, so a slow slide is visible before it becomes a crisis.

CF-23.445 §7.heading: CF-23.445 §7 Governance Disclosure Fields, Supporting Records, Accessibility, and Challenge-Pathway Usability
CF-23.445 §7.gloss: What the public report must actually show, broken out by family and urgency, so outsiders can see where matters are stuck rather than only a reassuring average.

CF-23.445 §8.heading: CF-23.445 §8 Contest-Integrity Monitoring Interface
CF-23.445 §8.gloss: Independent monitors read the performance data and ask the harder question: do the delays cluster where conflict, capture, or retaliation would predict?

CF-23.445 §9.heading: CF-23.445 §9 Non-Compliant Performance Patterns
CF-23.445 §9.gloss: Named failure shapes that are presumed non-compliant — chronic delay concentrated in emergency matters, backlogs that predictably defeat remedy, and unexplained publication delay on significant rulings.

CF-23.450.heading: CF-23.450: Forum Continuity
CF-23.450.gloss: **CF-23.450** states what forums must keep doing when normal operation breaks down — emergency conditions, missing key staff, no lawful panel available, or infrastructure failure. Procedure may be simplified; the right to contest a decision may not be erased.

CF-23.450 §1.heading: CF-23.450 §1 Rights-Floor Continuity Rule
CF-23.450 §1.gloss: Emergencies may simplify procedure; they may never erase the right to contest, the route to urgent relief, or the record that makes review possible.

CF-23.450 §2.heading: CF-23.450 §2 Continuity Modes
CF-23.450 §2.gloss: The named states a forum can be in, from Normal through Emergency and Fallback to Restoration. Moving between them must be triggered, recorded, and reversible.

CF-23.450 §3.heading: CF-23.450 §3 Activation Triggers
CF-23.450 §3.gloss: A continuity mode switches on only from a documented finding — no lawful panel can be formed, infrastructure is down, key staff are unavailable — not from general unease.

CF-23.450 §4.heading: CF-23.450 §4 Continuity Minimum Functions
CF-23.450 §4.gloss: The floor that survives any degraded mode: urgent intake, emergency relief, enough triage to spot Rights-Floor cases, and preservation of the record.

CF-23.450 §5.heading: CF-23.450 §5 Record Continuity and Custody
CF-23.450 §5.gloss: Even in emergency operation the docket must stay identifiable and the evidence chain unbroken, so the period can be reconstructed afterwards.

CF-23.450 §6.heading: CF-23.450 §6 Communication Duties
CF-23.450 §6.gloss: Parties must be told which mode is active, what still works, and what has been suspended. Silence during a crisis is itself a failure.

CF-23.450 §7.heading: CF-23.450 §7 Cross-System and Cross-Institution Coordination
CF-23.450 §7.gloss: When several bodies are affected at once, the plan must name who decides, how evidence is shared, who breaks a deadlock, and in what order normal operation resumes.

CF-23.450 §8.heading: CF-23.450 §8 Exercises and Testing
CF-23.450 §8.gloss: Continuity plans must be rehearsed against realistic scenarios — no independent panel available, a backlog surge, an outage — because an untested plan is an assumption.

CF-23.455.heading: CF-23.455: Fallback Operation
CF-23.455.gloss: **CF-23.455** is the temporary substitute for a forum that cannot sit — a reduced quorum, a backup venue, or a transfer away from a compromised family. It is temporary by design: it must record what it did and hand the matter back.

CF-23.455 §1.heading: CF-23.455 §1 Temporary Quorum and Provisional Authority
CF-23.455 §1.gloss: A smaller panel may sit temporarily only if the rule was written in advance, independence is preserved as far as possible, and a fuller panel reviews rights-affecting decisions promptly.

CF-23.455 §2.heading: CF-23.455 §2 Fallback Venues and Backup Forums
CF-23.455 §2.gloss: Each family names its backup in advance, along with how records and review rights travel with a transferred matter. Improvising a venue mid-crisis is what this prevents.

CF-23.455 §3.heading: CF-23.455 §3 Capture-Sensitive Fallback Operation
CF-23.455 §3.gloss: Where the emergency includes suspected capture or concealment, fallback must not leave control inside the suspected chain.

CF-23.455 §4.heading: CF-23.455 §4 Family-Capture Fallback Operation
CF-23.455 §4.gloss: The severe case: a whole family loses control of intake, panels, or publication. The record must state which family, on what basis, and what replaced it.

CF-23.460.heading: CF-23.460: Emergency Adjudication
CF-23.460.gloss: **CF-23.460** governs how urgent matters are decided while ordinary operation is degraded — what gets priority, who reviews emergency decisions while they are still in force, and how everything is reconciled once normal operation returns. An emergency is not a licence to decide without record or review.

CF-23.460 §1.heading: CF-23.460 §1 Emergency Triage Hierarchy
CF-23.460 §1.gloss: When there is not enough capacity for everything, this is the order: imminent loss of life or irreversible harm first, then evidence about to vanish, then coercive measures needing prompt review.

CF-23.460 §2.heading: CF-23.460 §2 Independent Review during Emergency Mode
CF-23.460 §2.gloss: Emergency powers are rechecked on a schedule while still in force — is the trigger still real, is the simplification still proportionate, is temporary authority hardening into permanent control?

CF-23.460 §3.heading: CF-23.460 §3 Restoration and Reconciliation
CF-23.460 §3.gloss: Once the trigger passes, ordinary rules resume, emergency orders that affected rights get reviewed, and delayed records are published or reconstructed.

CF-23.460 §4.heading: CF-23.460 §4 Post-Incident Review
CF-23.460 §4.gloss: Every activation ends with findings: what triggered it, what failed, what was used instead, and whether the Rights Floor actually held.

CF-23.460 §5.heading: CF-23.460 §5 Non-Compliant Emergency Patterns
CF-23.460 §5.gloss: The recognizable abuses — emergency mode extended indefinitely without reauthorization, emergency quorum used to concentrate lasting control, and loss of docket identity or evidence custody.

CF-23.465.heading: CF-23.465: Standard Records, Forms, and Evidence Artifacts
CF-23.465.gloss: **CF-23.465** is the paperwork floor. It gathers the record duties scattered across **CF-23.410** through **CF-23.460** into one minimum set — what must be captured, which fields it must carry, who may see it, and how long it is kept — so a decision can still be checked long after it was made.

CF-23.465 §1.heading: CF-23.465 §1 Minimum Record Set
CF-23.465 §1.gloss: The list of records every adopting entity must keep templates for, from intake through backup activation.

CF-23.465 §2.heading: CF-23.465 §2 Required Fields
CF-23.465 §2.gloss: What each record must carry — which body, which authority, when, who was responsible, and who was affected — so it remains interpretable years later.

CF-23.465 §3.heading: CF-23.465 §3 Access Classes
CF-23.465 §3.gloss: Records are tagged by who may see them: the parties, the public, or restricted review only. Tagging is decided by design rather than case by case.

CF-23.465 §4.heading: CF-23.465 §4 Evidence Artifact Handling
CF-23.465 §4.gloss: Evidence must keep its origin, handling history, and transformations attached, whether it is a physical object, a digital file, or a system log.

CF-23.465 §5.heading: CF-23.465 §5 Publication, Retention, and Reconciliation
CF-23.465 §5.gloss: Publication and retention rules are set in advance and kept consistent with the timeliness, continuity, and emergency requirements elsewhere in this family.

CF-23.465 §6.heading: CF-23.465 §6 Non-Compliant Record Patterns
CF-23.465 §6.gloss: The failures that make later review impossible: action with no attributable record, records omitting the review path, and forms that obscure how a matter was routed.

CF-23.470.heading: CF-23.470: Forum Staffing, Reserve Capacity, Shared Administration, Structural Review, and Structural Records
CF-23.470.gloss: **CF-23.470** covers whether a forum has enough qualified staff to function at all — how competence is defined, how support staff advance into adjudicative roles, what reserve capacity exists for surges, and which structural records prove it. Shared administration must not become a back door for steering cases.

CF-23.470 §2.heading: CF-23.470 §2 Reserve, Substitute, and Surge Capacity

CF-23.470 §3.heading: CF-23.470 §3 Shared Administration and Objective Assignment Safeguards

CF-23.470 §4.heading: CF-23.470 §4 Prohibited Staffing, Capacity, and Governance Patterns

CF-23.470 §5.heading: CF-23.470 §5 Structural Review and Revision Cadence

CF-23.470 §6.heading: CF-23.470 §6 Required Structural Records and Artifacts

CJS-5.110.heading: CJS-5.110: Oversight Leg Operations (oDef.2–oDef.6)
CJS-5.110.gloss: These clusters carry the **Oversight** leg into working terms: making a system explain itself, keeping enough record to reconstruct what happened, scaling who may see what, verifying claims independently, and keeping assurance itself resilient. They must be read together, because one strong control cannot rescue a weak link elsewhere.

CJS-5.110 §2.heading: CJS-5.110 §2 Oversight: Reflexive Transparency and Accountability Terms
CJS-5.110 §2.gloss: Authorities must hold themselves to standards at least as strict as those they impose on others. Exempting yourself from your own rule is the clearest sign the rule is not about safety.

CJS-5.110 §3.heading: CJS-5.110 §3 Oversight: Auditability and Reconstructability Terms (Annex)

CJS-5.110 §4.heading: CJS-5.110 §4 Oversight: Transparency Levels and Audit-Access Terms

CJS-5.110 §5.heading: CJS-5.110 §5 Oversight: Independent Verification and Claim-Integrity Terms

CJS-5.110 §6.heading: CJS-5.110 §6 Oversight: Integrity Assurance and Resilience Operations
CJS-5.110 §6.gloss: An integrity claim is only as good as the weakest link behind it — records, access controls, classification, and staffing all count, not just the part being advertised.

CJS-5.120.heading: CJS-5.120: Participation Leg Operations (oDef.7–oDef.10)
CJS-5.120.gloss: These clusters carry the **Participation** leg into working terms: who must be in the room for a decision to count, whether what is disclosed can actually be understood, whether important information is buried under trivia, and whether enough is visible to contest an outcome at all.

CJS-5.120 §10.heading: CJS-5.120 §10 Participation: Disclosure Sufficiency and Observability Terms
CJS-5.120 §10.gloss: Enough must be visible for someone outside to verify a claim and attribute a decision. Partial disclosure that cannot be checked is closer to marketing than accountability.

CJS-5.120 §7.heading: CJS-5.120 §7 Participation: Quorum and Participatory Legitimacy Terms
CJS-5.120 §7.gloss: Who must take part for a binding decision to count, and what makes that participation real rather than a formality with a predetermined outcome.

CJS-5.120 §8.heading: CJS-5.120 §8 Participation: Comprehensibility and Cognitive Accessibility Terms
CJS-5.120 §8.gloss: Disclosure that cannot be understood is not disclosure. Material information must be presented so the sentients it affects can actually follow it.

CJS-5.120 §9.heading: CJS-5.120 §9 Participation: Salience Integrity and Attention-Allocation Terms
CJS-5.120 §9.gloss: Systems that decide what gets seen first, often, rarely, or never — ranking, feeds, notifications, search order — exercise real power over participation, and this states the limits on it.

CJS-5.125.heading: CJS-5.125: Accountability Leg Operations (oDef.11–oDef.15)
CJS-5.125.gloss: These clusters carry the **Accountability** leg into working terms: how far authority may be concentrated, who must justify a decision and how heavily, what makes a procedure sound, who may authorize an override, and when a structure must be reviewed and corrected. The bigger the stake, the stronger each requirement becomes.

CJS-5.125 §11.heading: CJS-5.125 §11 Accountability: Distributed and Proportional Authority Terms

CJS-5.125 §11.2.heading: CJS-5.125 §11.2 Anti-Domination Conduct and Remediation Catalog

CJS-5.125 §12.heading: CJS-5.125 §12 Accountability: Burden-of-Justification and Constraint Terms
CJS-5.125 §12.gloss: Whoever restricts something carries the burden of justifying it — with the lightest effective measure, and with that justification refreshed rather than assumed to hold forever.

CJS-5.125 §13.heading: CJS-5.125 §13 Accountability: Procedural Integrity and Adjudication Terms
CJS-5.125 §13.gloss: The shared floor for fair process: notice, a real chance to respond, a reviewable decision, and enforcement proportionate to what actually happened.

CJS-5.125 §14.heading: CJS-5.125 §14 Accountability: Intervention Governance and Override-Authorization Terms
CJS-5.125 §14.gloss: When someone may override normal operation, who must authorize it, and what record that leaves. An override capability is necessary; an unlogged one is a back door.

CJS-5.125 §15.heading: CJS-5.125 §15 Accountability: Structural Review, Correction Urgency, and Disclosure Terms

CJS-5.130.heading: CJS-5.130: Continuity Aim Operations (oDef.16–oDef.21)
CJS-5.130.gloss: These clusters keep a system working — and keep it possible to leave — under dependency, change, stress, and attack: knowing what you depend on, being able to export and exit, retaining data for the right span, failing gracefully rather than catastrophically, being able to undo, and resisting deliberate abuse.

CJS-5.130 §16.heading: CJS-5.130 §16 Continuity: Dependency Integrity and Disclosure Terms
CJS-5.130 §16.gloss: If a system leans on something important, that reliance must be named, watched, and disclosed. Unmapped dependencies are how a single outage becomes a systemic failure.

CJS-5.130 §17.heading: CJS-5.130 §17 Continuity: Interoperability, Portability, and Exit-Integrity Terms
CJS-5.130 §17.gloss: Leaving must stay genuinely possible: real export, workable interfaces, and no design that makes departure technically available but practically impossible.

CJS-5.130 §18.heading: CJS-5.130 §18 Continuity: Data-Retention and Lifecycle-Integrity Terms
CJS-5.130 §18.gloss: How long data is kept, how it changes, what gets linked to what, and what deletion actually means — because retention decisions quietly determine what can be audited or abused later.

CJS-5.130 §19.heading: CJS-5.130 §19 Continuity: Graceful Degradation and Failure-Mode Integrity Terms
CJS-5.130 §19.gloss: Under partial failure a system must behave honestly: degrade visibly rather than pretend to work, and fail in a way that can be recovered from.

CJS-5.130 §20.heading: CJS-5.130 §20 Continuity: Reversibility and Containment Terms
CJS-5.130 §20.gloss: Design so that mistakes can be undone and damage stays local. Irreversible-by-default architecture converts every error into a permanent one.

CJS-5.130 §21.heading: CJS-5.130 §21 Continuity: Adversarial Robustness and Abuse-Resistance Terms
CJS-5.130 §21.gloss: Assume someone will actively try to misuse the system, including by exploiting its incentives rather than its code, and build defenses that survive that.

CJS-5.135.heading: CJS-5.135: Integrative Cross-Leg Operations (oDef.22–oDef.23)
CJS-5.135.gloss: Two clusters that no single Tetrad leg owns cleanly. Constrained secrecy sits between oversight and accountability: some investigations must stay quiet without becoming unreviewable. Intervention integrity sits between accountability and continuity: someone must be able to intervene in a running system without that power going unchecked.

CJS-5.135 §22.heading: CJS-5.135 §22 Integrative: Constrained-Secrecy and Protected-Investigation Terms
CJS-5.135 §22.gloss: Some work genuinely must stay quiet for a while. This states the limits: bounded scope, a defined end, and eventual disclosure — secrecy with an expiry date rather than a permanent shield.

CJS-5.135 §23.heading: CJS-5.135 §23 Integrative: Intervention and Override Integrity Terms
CJS-5.135 §23.gloss: Systems need a way to interrupt harm quickly, and that emergency stop must itself be accountable — otherwise the safety mechanism becomes the vulnerability.

CJS-5.140.heading: CJS-5.140: oDef Parse Mechanics
CJS-5.140.gloss: How to read each **oDef** entry: **What it is** says what the rule covers, **How to measure and assess** says what evidence to check and how reviewers verify it, and **What must hold** states the binding failure modes.
